arrival_seyda_neen:
Chapter 1: An Unexpected Arrival in Seyda Neen

Scotti found himself deposited on the docks of what the locals apparently call "Seyda Neen" with nothing but his common clothes, 87 gold pieces, an iron dagger he wouldn't know how to use if his life depended on it (which, given current circumstances, it very well might), and two mysterious items: a package for someone named Caius Cosades and directions to find him in Balmora.

The settlement appeared to be a modest fishing village with the standard Imperial colonial overlay — a Census and Excise Office, predictably bureaucratic in its positioning, and what looked like a tradehouse that might, if the gods were merciful, serve actual food. The architecture showed the usual provincial compromises: local materials pressed into Imperial service, with varying degrees of success.

Most concerning was the presence of several hostile creatures in the surrounding waters — slaughterfish and mudcrabs, if the Commission's provincial wildlife reports were accurate. Scotti made a mental note to avoid swimming at all costs.
infrastructure_concerns:
Initial Assessment of Seyda Neen Infrastructure:

The settlement appears to suffer from what can only be described as systemic connectivity failures. Navigation systems are non-functional, door mechanisms unresponsive, and the general flow of civic services appears to operate on principles wholly foreign to Imperial standards. 

Most concerning is the apparent abundance of hostile wildlife in the immediate vicinity — multiple varieties of slaughterfish and mudcrabs patrol the local waters, suggesting either inadequate pest control measures or a complete absence of municipal wildlife management. The local flora includes numerous species of fungi that, while possibly edible, are growing in completely unregulated fashion across the settlement.

Scotti made a mental note to recommend a full Commission inspection of the local building codes, assuming he survived long enough to file such a report.
first_paralysis:
Chapter 2: The Curious Case of Involuntary Stillness

It was at this moment that Scotti discovered one of the more unsettling aspects of life in Morrowind: the occasional, complete failure of one's basic locomotive functions. Whether this was due to some peculiar atmospheric condition, a curse inherent in the local soil, or simply the province's way of informing newcomers that they were not in the civilized portions of the Empire anymore, Scotti could not say.

What he could say was that standing immobile on a dock while a Wood Elf named Fargoth presumably watched his predicament with amusement was not covered in any Commission training manual he had ever read. The smell of salt and rotting fish, the ominous creaking of boats whose seaworthiness he seriously questioned, and the alien glow of fungal specimens that belonged in an alchemist's fever dream rather than municipal landscaping — all of it combined to create an atmosphere of profound unease.

Scotti began to suspect that his arrival in Morrowind was less a posting and more a sentence.
